meta.title: Attention Is All You Need
meta.claimSummary: The paper claims sequence transduction needs no recurrence. It held up.

items.statement: Positional encodings were learned in the original paper.

nodes.title: Dot products
nodes.hook: You need one operation before any of this makes sense.

spiral.intuition: A dot product asks how much two arrows point the same way.
spiral.concrete: For [1,0] and [1,1] the dot product is 1.
spiral.formal: a dot b equals the sum over i of a_i times b_i.

wrongTurn.belief: If you are thinking a dot product measures distance
wrongTurn.correction: It measures alignment. Two long vectors pointing the same way score high even when far apart.

mcq.stem: What is the dot product of two orthogonal vectors?

options.why: Perpendicular vectors share no component along each other, so every term cancels.
One is a unit vector dotted with itself; orthogonality removes the aligned part entirely.
That is the value when the vectors point the same way, where the cosine is one, not zero.

mcq.explanation: Orthogonal means no shared direction, so every term cancels and the sum is zero.

mcq.stem: What does a large positive dot product between two unit vectors indicate?

options.why: Alignment is exactly what the operation measures.

options.text: They are far apart in space
options.why: Plausible because both feel like similarity, but distance is a different operation; unit vectors are all the same length.
Plausible in general, but these are unit vectors, so magnitude is fixed at one.

mcq.explanation: For unit vectors the dot product is the cosine of the angle between them, so large positive means nearly parallel.

quiz.selfExplain: Conceptualize in one sentence why alignment and distance are different questions.
quiz.selfExplainAnswer: The dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way, so it is large when they align and zero when they are perpendicular.

nodes.title: Scaled dot-product attention
nodes.hook: Therefore the whole mechanism reduces to one weighted average.

spiral.intuition: Every token asks every other token a question and gets a weighted answer back.
spiral.concrete: With three tokens you compute nine scores, soften them into weights, and mix the values.
spiral.formal: Attention of Q, K, V is softmax of Q K transpose over root d_k, times V.

wrongTurn.belief: If you are thinking the scaling factor is there for numerical overflow
wrongTurn.correction: It is there because dot products of d_k-dimensional vectors have variance proportional to d_k, so the softmax saturates and gradients vanish.

diagram.alt: Q, K and V flowing through matmul, scale, softmax and matmul

mcq.stem: In attention, the scores QKᵀ are divided by the square root of what?

options.why: Each score sums d_k products, so its variance grows with d_k and the square root undoes that.
Length sets how many scores there are, not how large each individual score grows.
Heads split the model width, but each head scales by its own key dimension.

mcq.explanation: Queries are matched against keys, and the scale is the key dimension.

mcq.stem: Why is the score divided by the square root of the key dimension?

options.text: To keep the softmax out of its saturated region
options.why: Variance of the dot product grows with d_k, which flattens gradients once softmax saturates.

options.text: To normalize the attention weights so they sum to one
options.why: Genuinely tempting, but the softmax already guarantees that; the scaling happens before it.

options.text: To reduce the quadratic cost of attention
options.why: A real motivation for other attention variants, but a scalar divide changes no complexity.

mcq.explanation: Large d_k inflates dot-product variance, pushing softmax into regions with very small gradients. Dividing by the square root holds the variance roughly constant.

quiz.selfExplain: Conceptualize in one sentence what breaks if the scaling is removed.
quiz.selfExplainAnswer: Dot products grow with the key dimension, and dividing by its square root keeps the scores in a range where softmax still spreads attention instead of saturating.

nodes.title: Multi-head attention
nodes.hook: But one attention pattern cannot represent several relationships at once.

spiral.intuition: Run the whole thing several times in parallel and staple the answers together.
spiral.concrete: Eight heads of 64 dimensions each reassemble into the same 512 you started with.
spiral.formal: Concatenate the head outputs and apply one more learned projection.

wrongTurn.belief: If you are thinking more heads means more parameters
wrongTurn.correction: The per-head dimension shrinks to compensate, so total cost is roughly unchanged.

mcq.stem: What happens to the head outputs before the final projection?

options.why: Keeping them side by side lets the learned projection decide how to mix what each head found.
Averaging would blur what each head specialised in before any learned weighting sees it.
Summing mixes the heads with fixed equal weights, which is the job the output projection learns instead.

mcq.explanation: They are joined along the feature axis, restoring the model dimension.

mcq.stem: What does splitting attention across heads buy you?

options.text: Several relationship types represented at once
options.why: Each head can specialize in a different subspace.
Understandable given the smaller per-head dimension, but the heads run in parallel so the total is comparable.
Plausible if you conflate heads with sequence position, but heads partition features, not positions.

mcq.explanation: Each head projects into its own subspace, so different heads can attend on different criteria simultaneously.

quiz.selfExplain: Conceptualize in one sentence why one head is not enough.
quiz.selfExplainAnswer: Each head can attend to a different kind of relationship, and concatenating them lets the projection combine several views of the sequence at once.

nodes.title: Positional encoding
nodes.hook: But attention alone is blind to order, so position has to be injected.

spiral.intuition: Attention sees a bag of tokens, so order must be added to the tokens themselves.
spiral.concrete: Each position gets a fixed pattern of sines and cosines at different frequencies.
spiral.formal: PE at position pos and dimension 2i is the sine of pos over 10000 to the 2i over d_model.

wrongTurn.belief: If you are thinking the encodings are learned
wrongTurn.correction: The original paper used fixed sinusoids and reported that learned embeddings performed about the same.

mcq.stem: What kind of positional encodings did the original paper use?

options.why: The paper chose fixed sinusoids, hoping they extrapolate to lengths unseen in training.
The paper tried learned embeddings and found them about equal, but kept sinusoids for extrapolation.
Relative schemes arrived in later work; the original added absolute encodings to the input.

mcq.explanation: Fixed sinusoids were chosen partly in the hope of extrapolating to longer sequences.

mcq.stem: Why does a transformer need positional information at all?

options.text: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant on its own
options.why: Shuffling the inputs shuffles the outputs identically, so order carries no signal.
Tempting, but softmax is applied to scores; the missing order is upstream of it.
Plausible-sounding, but residuals are elementwise and preserve whatever ordering exists.

mcq.explanation: Attention computes a weighted sum over a set. Permute the inputs and you permute the outputs, so nothing in the operation encodes where a token sat.

quiz.selfExplain: Conceptualize in one sentence what a transformer would confuse without positional encoding.
quiz.selfExplainAnswer: Attention itself ignores order, so position has to be added to the inputs or every permutation of the sentence would look identical.
